game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It’s timely that Orwell, the first game from Australian start-up Osmotic Studios delves into the muddy waters of government surveillance of its citizens, with the increasing nature of real world democracies doing the very same as they grapple with a world that is always connected and communicating.

Orwell opens with a deadly bombing in a public square that the player is tasked to investigate. This is achieved via a secret program codenamed Orwell, which allows an anonymous user, with the oversight of a supervisor, to snoop through social media posts, personal computers, bank statements and private correspondence of the suspects and associates.

My initial surveillance began with a singular suspect who had been caught by CCTV in the surrounding area and who had previously been arrested for attacking a police officer. My supervisor seemed to believe in this system, that malice lurked in unseen corners and that everyone was a potential threat.

From this one suspect a deeper conspiracy of activists emerged, and concerns of the erosion of liberties that were taken for granted by the citizens both fortified and weakened the idea of Orwell.

Continuing to spy on the fellow member’s activist group Thought reveals snippets of conversation that follow a story of mistrust of government and the over-reach of surveillance. Your actions, and inaction can and do have major consequences for those that you survey – and decisions on what you choose to upload to Orwell through a simple drag and drop interface can have fatal consequences and lock you to certain storylines.

Sifting through the large amount of data that the unknowing citizens freely make available reveals a story of love, betrayal, anger and sacrifice. I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time.

Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions.

The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. 

The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time.

8.2/10.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time. 8.2/10.

review_text_raw:
[quote][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/7871885/]Follow our curator page:[b] OCG-Curations[/b] if you like and want to see more reviews like this one.[/url][/quote]

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
Orwell takes place in a distopian near future in the fictional city of Bonton in The Nation. Orwell is the codename of a vastly advanced surveilance system. They outsource investigations to outsiders of the nation - you! It is your task to spy on suspects and inform the government of what is going on. Basically, you roleplay as "Mr. FBI Man".

[h1]The Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Interesting Story[/b] - The game is divided into five chapters, each representing a day in game. I won't be spoiling anything here so there isn't much to say, but I will state my overall impression. The story is good! If you take everything at face value you'll be in for a surprise when you realise this game is not as shallow as it may seem. Each chapter unveils another layer of mystery. There are also three endings (more on that later).

[*][b]Some Replayability[/b] - Every chapter has a few endings (usually two or three). After you finish the game, you may choose to replay starting from any chapter (subsequent ones are erased). Most unique paths you can take are linked to an achievement, so 100%-ing the game is pretty much just exploring every possibility. Don't get too exited though, as that took me about 8 hours and two playthroughs (but in the second one I did consult a guide to save time).

[*][b]Clean UI[/b] - I really like the clean, very intuitive interface. Which is good, considering as this UI is basically the whole game itself. The only downside is that it does not have a dark mode for playing at night, but it's not a dealbreaker.
[/list]

[h1]The Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]Hand Holding[/b] - You give information to Orwell by drag and dropping data chunks from your spy browser to the Orwell app. They are automatically outlined for you, which seems stupid, but it's a necesarry evil if you think about the programmers. However, one thing I don't like are the special chunks - the conflicts are highlighted in yellow, even if you didn't find both. This makes you extra careful before uploading as one makes the other invalid. This is how the story branches, but if you think about it it's a little stupid. How does the browser know about the conflict if you didn't access the other data chunk yet? This should be up to you - the "detective" to figure out. I wish they were all blue all the time, or turn yellow only after discovering both.

[*][b]Choices Almost Don't Matter[/b] - Remember when I said chapters? Well... they're pretty much isolated instances. Outcomes are mentioned from one to another, but only through slight dialogue changes. But the story progresses the same no matter what you do, until you reach chapter five and finally get to choose an ending.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Orwell is a good game because it explores an interesting concept and offers a good story to boot. While it's not as mindbending as I first expected, I still recommended it as a very interactive visual novel. If the topic interests you and don't mind the short playtime, this is a good game to pick up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is a truly amazing game. It really gets you thinking about mass surveillance. It's hardly impartial, but you get to see both the good and the bad aspects. If you have an interest in privacy, play this game. If you have never given it much thought, play this game. If you've ever said 'I have nothing to hide, it doesn't matter', play this game.

Pros:
- really gets you thinking about mass surveillance
- you control how the story unfolds based on what information you pass on to the government
- the story has some really great twists and surprises that I didn't see coming

Cons:
- Playing involves dragging and dropping pieces of information onto profiles of people you're investigating, but sometimes the drag and drop function is finicky, I occasionally had to retry multiple times to grab a piece of data. Not a big issue, but a minor annoyance.

A warning to achievement hunters: *do not* look at any 100% achievement guides before playing, they will ruin the story. You'll need 2 playthroughs anyway. Just play through normally the first time and you should be able to get all remaining achievements the second time.

Verdict: 10/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

I must say I never heard from that game, after it pops up on Steam at its release date.

And I'm suprised to say, that this game catched me aloen by its name!

I awaited a Big Brother game ... and I got a Big Brother game ... a game, where you can be Big Brother yourself.

You take control of a new surveilance system called Orwell to find the people responsible for a terror bombing.
Fot that you can check websites, 'listen' to calls and chats and search through phones and computers.

- Fitting graphic style and background music
- Good story
- 'Just one more minute/level/stage'
- Different endings and outcomes of story parts

Neutral:
- 4-6 hour for a single walkthrough
- Balanced 'Cliché' and 'Suprised' moments/characters

Cons:
- A bit to simple gameplay (there are only some situations, where it is a bit hard to decide between different choices)
- No 'dead ends'
- Linear story progress

As this game offers its first (of five) episodes for free as a demo (works also as a tutorial), you can easily test out, if you like its gameplay. The initial price of around 10 € is very fair, so do the devs a favor if you like the demo and buy it directly. ;)

I really hope the devs use the base concept/gameplay for some more games! I really like that detective style of conecting clues. But at the same time I hope they expend the concept with video footage to analyze, dead ends, more conflicting clues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wrote this review after 3 episodes, I might change it later.

Orwell is an interesting game about collecting personal data from people through various means (social media, dating sites, phone calls etc.) and investigating to find the terrorist/s that plant bombs in public places. The gameplay reminds me a lot of Analogue : Hate Story, which is a good sign. Every document gives you new informations, that leads you to new documents etc.

Overall the writing is very solid and believable, you can only see typed messages but they all express the character's personality : the lawyer is writing slowly with perfect punctuation, the young activist uses slang and typos etc. Sometimes there are some blatant shortcuts designed for exposition (a conversation with an unknown person that starts with "What can I do for you, Susan Mills, my best friend from Hugand University ?") but it didn't bother me too much.

What bothers me however is how much the game holds your hand. You can only select a few informations and only about the suspect "du jour". Several times I thought "Wow, Alan is very suspect !" but I couldn't get any informations about him until the next day where I'm told "Today we'll focus on Alan, he's suspect". Am I the investigator or just a goddamn clerk ?

It led to a very aggravating moment where I had to chose between two options, I took the wrong one and innocent people died. To add insult to injury, my sidekick had the nerve to patronize me "What did we do wrong ? If we had taken the other option, this could have been avoided". I think it was meant to emotionally disturb me and make me think that this investigation method is fundamentally flawed, on top of being ethically reprehensible. But instead all I could think was "F*ck you, all informations you ALLOWED me to get pointed at the first option being the good one. You think you're cleverly ambiguous but you're just a cheap mystery novel deliberately misleading the audience to make the plot last long enough".

In conclusion, an extremely lukewarm approval, that might lead to a disapproval if they keep doing this in future episodes. I don't want to replay this game as it feels like Telltale's Walking Dead, where the illusion of choice disappears at the second playthrough where different choices don't impact as much as they seemed.

EDIT : I finished the 5 chapters, I keep my extremely uncommitted approval (lets say 50.1/100).
What limits this game the most is its linearity. I compared it to a mystery novel, it's even worse in late episodes, they want you to suspect specific people in specific orders punctuated by specific twists. You learn in chapter 5 crucial informations that you had no reason not to discover in chapters 1 and 2, since you follow the exact same protocol except the game deliberately kept informations away from you in order to make the game last 5 chapters.

The game also has the nerve to make this railroad look like a social commentary. "You've been chasing the wrong people the entire time, this is the proof that Orwell is unreliable !". Yeah but no, this is just proof that you're putting arbitrary limitations for the sake of the narrative. And even with that, Orwell did better than any other investigation method. Call it unethical, dangerous, tyrannical if you want, but it gets sh*t done and saved lives, and would have done even better without the railroad.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is very unique and interesting, it is not very long but it is a game that makes you think for a long periods of time.

Pros:
Amazing plot, there are alternative paths
Good choice with factions, there is no 'Good' guys vs 'Bad' guys feeling. Its up to you to create who is 'Good' and who is 'Bad.' This is very good since most recent games are forced to have forced 'Political Correctness.' This game is not bias in politics, and gives choice to player to do what they want and judge how they want. (Think of this game like in Far Cry 4 in terms of factions, you get to judge who is more 'right' or less 'wrong')
Lots of data-based reading (if you are okay with reading lots of things for lore, this is a type of game for you)
Lots of characters to anaylize and discover
Price is very cheap during discount
When you finish the game get ready to have several minutes or hours of heavy philosophical discussion with your mind

Neutral:
They could of added a bit more creative names for the country and political party in the game, all the other nations in game got more creative names while you just live in 'The Nation.' Sadly no Oceania vibes
Pretty good music, I really love intro music but music gets a bit repetitive during the Missions.

Cons:
You have to finish the game to go back to 'Days', if you accidently did something wrong you have to stay all day
I wish more touch was added to characters that got prisoned etc., it just feels awkward not getting a lot of info about them after a certain mission.
Sadly the game is not very long, if you play entire day you can finish the game in one or 2 days (Game is made of 5 Days)

The game is very good, and you should buy it for a nice philosophical experience with your mind.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Acting as a sort of Big Brother VN version of Deathtrap Dungeon, you are the "villain" behind the screen of a dystopian (?) surveillance project. I add a question mark beside the "dystopian" descriptor, because in a fairly surprising subversion of expectations, the group of people you are watching are every bit as awful, shallow, annoying, and at least in a couple of cases, actually dangerous and crazy as to justify using such a program. 

In any other hands, this game would have the government you're working for be up to unspeakable acts beyond justification and the collection of rabble rousing, blue haired agitators you're investigating would be perfect, selfless angels,  with maybe a few thin personal flaws to give them the pretense of being attractively tragic and interesting. In this game, however, they are every bit as annoying, shallow, self important and deluded as the ones that currently exist IRL, complete with being pilled out on a pantry's worth of anti-depressants and rife with anger management issues and savior complexes. 

I was actually quite shocked at this development, considering the "modern audiences" presentation that this game and its sequel give off; the character portraits you can choose from in both are allergic to White people and the art style throughout is comprised of hideous, polygonal corpo-art. But if you are interested in busting leftoids, who are rarely represented accurately in this medium, or indeed at all, give this game and its sequel a go. The "mysteries" aren't terribly interesting, as they mostly revolve around made up political disputes between blandly named stand in's, but there is some catharsis to be had in sending loud mouthed, Hot Topic "punk rock" brainlets (not to mention the group's couple of older academics and lawyers of dubious ancestry who act as organizer and funder) a candy-gram from a SWAT team.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Play as yourself using a government surveillance system, Orwell. Investigate the public and private lives of suspect individuals and citizens to find the one responsible for a series of terror attacks and prevent more from ever happening. Moral dilemma nothing, create profiles and collect data to submit to your superiors to bring individuals in for questioning, arrest, or deliver your own type of justice. No one is completely innocent. 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a text based 7+ hour game with 5 chapters and 3 endings. Typically, reading the description of the game it would be natural to suspect Orwell is about learning the evils of government surveillance systems and their terrible effects, but both sides of the issue are shown and the game is very morally ambiguous. There are no right or wrong answers to your choices and honestly, it made the game more interesting. I took my time and ended up playing 9 hours straight instead of the 2-3 I planned. Orwell is remarkably immersive for a game and I definitely recommend you play it if you’re even slightly interested in the story.
